purpose: Current public examples for the societal responsibility of language braid; contextual evidence, not case evidence or political endorsement.
political_neutrality: Examples test reciprocity and power-of-language claims; no electoral recommendation, fitness judgment, motive inference or causal finding.

sources.speaker: Donald J. Trump
sources.title: President Trump on 60 Minutes: “There Was Tremendous Camaraderie”
sources.supports: Trump publicly described Democratic hate speech as dangerous for the country.
sources.limits: White House-produced summary of an interview; use for the President's quoted position, not as independent proof about causes of political violence.
sources.quotation_used: the hate speech of the Democrats

sources.speaker: Donald J. Trump
sources.title: Donald Trump remarks with Mark Rutte
sources.supports: Trump used the term Dumocrats and said Democrats were dumb.
sources.limits: Transcript supports wording; it does not establish effects, motive or audience interpretation.

sources.speaker: Reuters reporting
sources.title: Republicans seize on Michigan progressives' wins, but party is split on socialism message
sources.locator: Article discussion of Trump labels and interviews with competitive House campaigns
sources.supports: Trump used Communist/Socialist labels against named Democratic/progressive candidates; Republican campaigns differed on use of the socialism message.
sources.limits: Campaign-strategy reporting; does not establish that the labels accurately describe any candidate's ideology.

sources.speaker: Reuters reporting with quoted Trump posts and White House response
sources.title: Trump says 'seditious' Democrats urging US troops to refuse illegal orders should face death
sources.locator: Trump posts and White House clarification
sources.supports: Trump called six Democratic lawmakers traitors, described their conduct as seditious and potentially punishable by death; White House later said he was not seeking their execution.
sources.limits: Preserve the lawmakers' underlying message and the White House clarification; article does not establish that rhetoric caused later violence.

sources.speaker: Donald J. Trump
sources.title: Remarks to Supporters Prior to the Storming of the United States Capitol
sources.publication: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara
sources.locator: Closing portion and earlier march instruction
sources.supports: The same speech included both fight-like-hell language and an instruction to march peacefully and patriotically.
sources.limits: Transcript establishes wording and context, not a standalone legal conclusion about intent, causation or liability.

use_rule: Retain both supporting and materially qualifying context. These sources illustrate language/power reciprocity and do not determine the book's private final reader question or any election choice.
